messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leila, a sixty-nine-year-old fast-food worker, had spent thirty-two years behind the counter of the same diner in a small Midwestern city, her hands moving automatically over the register and the fry station while she greeted regulars by name. That world ended fourteen months ago, when a customer—a man she had served nearly every morning for six months—began waiting for her after her shifts. At first she told herself he was just lonely. Then he started leaving notes on her car, describing what she had worn that day. Then he was outside her apartment building at three in the morning, standing under the streetlight, watching her bedroom window.

The night that became the event she could not stop reliving happened in late October. She had finished her shift at eleven and walked to her car in the employee lot. He was already there, kneeling by her driver’s side door, and when she saw him she froze. He did not move toward her. He simply looked up and said, very softly, “You smell like grease and onions and I love it.” She could smell it too—the fryer oil that had soaked into her uniform, the sharp tang of onions on her hands, the sourness of her own sweat from a double shift. She ran back inside and called the police, but by the time they arrived, he was gone. The restraining order she obtained did not stop the notes, or the calls at odd hours, or the feeling that she was being watched wherever she went.

Leila had never thought of herself as a fearful person, but now she could not sleep through the night without waking multiple times to check that the deadbolt was still thrown, that the chain was still on. She had developed a ritual: before bed she walked through every room, testing every window lock, then checked them all again an hour later when she inevitably woke. Her husband, Rashid, had stopped asking about it. He just lay in the dark while she moved through the apartment, listening to the click of the locks.

At work, she had begun scanning every customer before she greeted them. She watched their hands, their eyes, the way they stood. She had learned to read threat in the smallest details—a man holding his coffee cup too tightly, a woman who lingered at the counter a moment too long. She could not stop doing it. It felt like survival. But it also felt like losing herself. She used to be the one who joked with the bus drivers and remembered the schoolteachers’ orders. Now she was the one who flinched when a customer raised their hand to point at the menu.

The memory of that night came to her not in images but in smells. Sometimes, when the fryer oil was fresh and the onions hit the grill, she would be back in that parking lot, her heart hammering, the man’s voice in her ear. Other times she could recall the whole thing—the cold air, the streetlight, his face—but felt nothing at all, as if she were watching a movie about someone else. That numbness frightened her more than the fear. She had told her daughter once, “It’s like it happened to a different woman, and I don’t know where she went.” The story of what happened felt so extreme that sometimes she had to remind herself it was real. She would pull out the police report and read it, just to confirm that the events actually occurred.

She had stopped thinking about the event deliberately. If a thought about that night surfaced—while she was chopping tomatoes, while she was waiting for the bus—she pushed it away immediately. She was certain that if she let herself really think about it, she would fall apart completely. She would not be able to go to work. She would not be able to leave the house. She had come to believe that her mind was fragile, that the memory was a trap door, and that one wrong step would send her through it.

She had also come to believe that people could not be trusted. Not just the man who stalked her, but everyone. The neighbor who smiled at her in the hallway—was he watching her? The new cashier who asked too many questions—was she reporting back to someone? Leila knew, intellectually, that this was not rational. But the feeling was stronger than reason. She had stopped going to the mosque, stopped visiting her sister, stopped walking to the corner store. Her world had shrunk to the apartment, the diner, and the bus route between them.

What finally brought her to a clinic was not the fear or the checking or the mistrust. It was the moment last week when her manager called her into the office and said customers had complained that she seemed “unfriendly.” Leila had stood there, holding her order pad, and realized she could not remember the last time she had looked a customer in the eye without scanning them for danger. She had not known who she was anymore. She had told the intake worker that she wanted to go back to being the person who smiled at strangers, but she did not know if that person still existed. What frightened her most was the possibility that the woman in the parking lot had not just been frightened, but erased.
